\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered
with a median error of \ErrRep{}\% $[\ErrRepLo{}, \ErrRepHi{}]$
($n=\ErrRepN{}$), one-directional: models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than
requested, never systematically more.

Within $k\le32$ that deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating --- not what
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. A constant fits the panel's median count
above $k\!=\!6$ with residual sum of squares \ShapeSatSSE{} against
\ShapePropSSE{} for $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$, in \ShapePropModels{} of
\ErrNModels{} checkpoints (S10): the count tracks the request, so no horizon lies
inside this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it, post hoc, to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on the \HzNModels{}
checkpoints whose decoders admit utterances that long (S10). Tracking stops: the
repeated median sits at \HzMedRepKLo{} at $k\!=\!48$ and \HzMedRepKHi{} at
$k\!=\!128$ while the request triples and the control climbs \HzMedCtlKLo{} to
\HzMedCtlKHi{}. Of \HzNGen{} generations \HzExclCap{} hit our budget and
\HzExclDegen{} were degenerate, leaving \HzNCellLo{}--\HzNCellHi{} per cell;
dropping truncated items is conservative, their counts being censored downward.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
so these decoders have a general utterance-length ceiling and the reportable
quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out. Fitting $\hat c(k)=\hat
K(1-e^{-k/\hat K})$ over the combined ladder --- $\hat K$ a saturation scale read
off counts, \emph{not} the theorem's $N^\ast$, a function of the unmeasured $q$
--- gives $\hat K_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ $[\HzNRepLo{},\HzNRepHi{}]$ against
$\hat K_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$: repetition
lowers the counting horizon \HzRatio{}-fold, saturating just past where our
ladder stopped, which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

The panel is not unanimous, and the exception is informative: intervals are
disjoint for \HzSepNames{}, while \HzRevNames{} shows \emph{no} repeated-side
saturation within $k\le128$ and inverts the ratio --- the same checkpoint that
shows no deficit at $k\le32$ (Table~\ref{tab:models}), a conditional theorem
behaving conditionally. The judge's bias points the same way as the effect (S9),
making \HzRatio{} an upper bound.

What degrades with $k$ is reliability, not proportion: the exactly-right share
falls from \ExactRepKLo{}\% at $k\!=\!\ExactRepKLoVal{}$ to \ExactRepKHi{}\% at
$k\!=\!\ExactRepKHiVal{}$, for word, sentence and place-value units alike.
Because the claim is about models, not about our corpus, we take the checkpoint
as the unit of replication, reducing each to its own repeated-minus-control
difference. The exactly-correct rate favours the control in all \CkExactN{} (mean
\CkExact{} points $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$); the median-error gap is
positive in \CkErrNPos{} of \CkErrN{}, zero in \ErrBestModel{}. Those six
cluster into \FamExactN{} families, so the effective replicate count is nearer
\FamExactN{}: per family the exact-rate gap is \FamExact{} points, range
$[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, positive in all \FamExactN{}. At either level
the panel is too small for significance testing --- the exact signed-rank floor
at $n\!=\!6$ is $0.031$ and no multiplicity correction clears $0.05$ (S11) --- so
we rest on effect sizes and their consistency.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, differing only in that the $k$ copies of one word
become non-adjacent ones. Were the failure about length, attention span or
exposure bias, the curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median
control error is \ErrCtl{}\% $[\ErrCtlLo{}, \ErrCtlHi{}]$ over $n=\ErrCtlN{}$
generations, at every $k$ up to $32$, for every model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings --- \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin correctly nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- the residual \CtlMissPct{}\% carry
genuine truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

One caveat belongs here, not in a limitation list: above $k\!=\!8$ the control's
fillers cycle a pool of eight, making that contrast period-$1$ against
period-$8$. Where controls carry no repetition at all --- $k\le8$ here, and the
whole extension ladder, whose $146$-word pool is never cycled --- the
dissociation survives: \ApLoRep{}\% against \ApLoCtl{}\% exact at $k\le8$, and
median error \ApHiMedRep{} against \ApHiMedCtl{} at $k\ge48$. Two further
rivals, improbability and an acoustic attractor, fail their own predictions
(S8).

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than non-repetitive text of the same length does. We
count states by the effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ of the trajectory
over normalised singular values and report the \emph{capacity gain}
$\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain; the gap is positive in all
\CkCapN{} checkpoints (mean \CkCap{} $[\CkCapLo{},\CkCapHi{}]$, $p=\CkCapP{}$)
but varies fourfold across them (SD \CkCapSD{}), so the mechanism is general in
direction, not in magnitude.

An obvious objection is circularity: rendering \emph{very} sixteen times really
does produce monotonous audio, so a low-rank trajectory might follow from the
stimulus rather than lost capacity. It does not --- covarying out realised output
diversity leaves the ratio at \CapAdjRatio{}, and restricting to correctly
rendered items at \CapCorrRatio{}, though that filter is not like-for-like
(\ExactCtl{}\% of controls survive it against \ExactRep{}\% of repeated items).
The gain stays \emph{positive} in \CapPosModels{} of \ErrNModels{}: at $k\le32$
repetition slows state acquisition without halting it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}'s premise holds only approximately --- renormalised
over the $k$ repeated key columns the most-attended occurrence takes
$\ShareMaxK{}/k$ of the block's mass at worst, so $\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$ nats
(S4) --- and its dose-response prediction fails outright. \emph{Within} a
$(\text{model},k)$ cell, items with flatter attention are counted \emph{better},
not worse ($r=\DilR{}$ $[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$, \DilCells{} cells, all
\DilNAgainst{} measures agreeing; controls at $\DilCtlR{}$; S12). We record this
as disconfirming: whatever selects which generations fail is not the degree of
dilution, and an observational design cannot say whether peaked attention instead
follows from a stalled decoder. Qwen3-TTS fuses text and acoustic embeddings and
cannot be checked.
